# Page language and language versions

Google determines a page's language for indexing from its content, not from hreflang or a language code in the URL, and its internationalisation talk said each page is annotated with only one language in the index (said at the event, not in Google's docs). Pages should therefore make their target language obvious and avoid mixing languages, and pages that translate only the template around untranslated main content are near-duplicates that Google may cluster. Each language version needs its own URL, because Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses without an Accept-Language header and versions switched by cookie, in place or by redirect may not all be crawled; a community speaker showed that a language selector built as a button leaves the whole alternate-language cluster without crawlable links. Google called language and country among its most important signals since its early days, and said index selection weights language so the index does not turn into an English one; in under-served languages such as Basque that makes lower-quality documents more likely to be selected and gives new local content a good chance to replace spam (the index-selection details were said at the event, not in Google's docs). Author's view: an orphaned language cluster is a case of Day 1's point that pages with no internal links depend on sitemaps and are found slowly. Day 3 showed the query side: detecting a query's language is Google's first step in understanding almost any query, and at retrieval Google matches results to the user's language wherever possible. A brand-only query does not reveal the language, so Google falls back on location and browser settings and sometimes shows the wrong language version; Google's help says the results language comes from the query, the user's language setting, the device's languages and location. Google called a missing result in a user's language an opportunity for whoever targets those words. Google said on Day 2 that working out a site's localized pages and which countries it targets is one of the difficult, complex tasks for it in indexing.

Based on: `D2-C585`, `D2-C584`, `D2-C586`, `D2-C587`, `D2-C588`, `D2-C589`, `D2-C366`, `D2-C560`, `D2-C561`, `D2-C187`, `D2-C649`, `D2-C654`, `D2-C651`, `D2-C652`, `D2-C650`, `D2-C690`, `D2-C691`, `D2-C189`, `D1-C067`, `D3-C006`, `D3-C080`, `D3-C007`, `D3-C008`, `D3-C009`, `D3-C090`, `D3-C092`, `D3-C081`, `D2-C961`.

## What to do

- Give every language version its own crawlable URL and link the versions with plain `<a href>` language selectors, never cookie-, script- or Accept-Language-based switching.
- Translate the whole page, template included, and keep one language per page; large untranslated blocks blur the language Google detects.
- Do not rely on hreflang or a language code in the URL to declare a page's language; the content decides.
- In under-served languages, publish content written for that market rather than machine translation at scale: the lower selection bar still comes with spam checks.
- Annotate language versions with hreflang and offer a visible language switcher, so brand searches reach the right version.

## Shown and said at the event

- **[Slide]** A market or language selector built as a button works for users but leaves the whole cluster of alternate-language pages without crawlable links, so the cluster is orphaned for Google.
  > "The nav works perfectly for users, and the entire alternate-language cluster is orphaned."
  <br><sub>`D2-C187` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · consistent with Google docs · [Link best practices for Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/links-crawlable) · Extends [D1-C115](../sessions/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Canonical links between different language versions of a page are a misuse: if a search engine accepted such a canonical group, only one language version would rank.

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation says Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses and sends no Accept-Language header, so pages that change content or redirect by the visitor's perceived country or language may not have every version crawled, indexed or ranked; it recommends separate URLs annotated with hreflang.
  <br><sub>`D2-C561` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [How Google crawls locale-adaptive pages](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/locale-adaptive-pages), [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites) · Used by `DEV-INT-01`, `DEV-INT-02`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's hreflang guide says pages that translate only the template (navigation, footer) around main content in one language still count as duplicates, because localized versions are duplicates only if the main content stays untranslated; it recommends hreflang for such pages.
  <br><sub>`D2-C589` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-07`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Help says the language a query is typed in is an important factor in choosing the language of results, alongside interface and device language, location and site owners' annotations, and that Google may also show results in other languages when they are helpful or when there is not enough information in the query's language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C604` · Google Search Help · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [How Google knows what language to show in search results](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/13511324?hl=en)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Help says the language of search results is chosen from the language of the query, the user's Google language setting, the device's languages and the user's location, which helps when a word such as 'taxi' is the same in several languages.
  <br><sub>`D3-C090` · Google Search Help · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [How Google knows what language to show in search results](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/13511324?hl=en)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to multi-regional and multilingual sites says Google Search tries to find pages that match the language of the searcher, and that geotargeting a site to one country can improve its rankings there at the expense of other locales.
  <br><sub>`D3-C092` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites)</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** Build market and language selectors as plain `<a href>` links to each alternate URL, not buttons or script handlers; otherwise the language versions have no internal links and depend on sitemaps to be found, which is slow.
  <br><sub>`D2-C189` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript · Extends [D1-C067](../sessions/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-06`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Because Google reads a page's language from its content and stores one language per page, translate templates (navigation, footer, buttons, legal notices) together with the main text; large untranslated blocks risk the page being annotated with the wrong language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C590` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · Used by `DEV-INT-07`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** List language variants such as fr-FR and fr-BE or de-DE and de-CH separately in a site's language inventory, and give each its own vocabulary and spelling review instead of reusing one translation for every country.
  <br><sub>`D2-C642` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Sites with several language versions should not leave brand searches to chance: annotate the versions with hreflang and offer a visible language switcher, because Google may have only the user's location and browser settings to choose a version.
  <br><sub>`D3-C010` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · Used by `DEV-INT-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Make each page's language and target country unambiguous (one main language per page, hreflang between versions, local prices, addresses and shipping details), because Google applies language and country already at retrieval, before ranking.
  <br><sub>`D3-C086` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · Used by `DEV-INT-07`</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-CAN-06`: Do not canonicalise one language version to another; connect them with hreflang
- Requirement `DEV-INT-01`: Give every language and country version its own URL
- Requirement `DEV-INT-02`: Do not redirect visitors automatically by IP address or browser language
- Requirement `DEV-INT-03`: Make hreflang complete: a self-reference, return links and fully qualified URLs
- Requirement `DEV-INT-06`: Build language and market selectors as `<a href>` links to each alternate URL
- Requirement `DEV-INT-07`: Make each page's language unambiguous by translating the template with the main content
- Glossary term *hreflang*
- Glossary term *Query understanding*
